run_benchmark_seeds.py:328 calls stats.wilcoxon(mogp_vals, base_vals) with NO keyword arguments, so scipy 1.17.1 defaults apply: zero_method='wilcox', correction=False, alternative='two-sided', method='auto'.
--seeds default is [0, 1, 2] (run_benchmark_seeds.py:547); MIN_SEEDS_FOR_POWER = 6 (line 272). Archived runs used 7 and 10 seeds, giving n_pairs = 7 and 5 respectively.

no ties, no zeros: scipy method='auto' uses the exact branch for n <= 50 and the normal approximation for n >= 51 (the test is on len(d) BEFORE zeros are dropped); the selector reproduced scipy's auto p-value on 59/59 sizes

WITH a tie in |d|: scipy method='auto' uses an exhaustive sign-flip PERMUTATION test for n in 2..13 and the normal approximation for n >= 14 (2**13 = 8192 <= the default 9999 resamples, so the permutation branch is exhaustive and deterministic, never Monte-Carlo). On 9 of those 12 sizes the permutation p-value is the ONLY one matching auto, so the branch is identified unambiguously and not by coincidence.

a single ZERO difference (with zero_method='wilcox') also forces the permutation branch for n <= 13, even though the zero is then dropped from the statistic; with no ties among the surviving |d| the two branches coincide numerically (12 of 18 probed sizes), so the override is invisible in the p-value but must still be implemented to stay right when ties and zeros occur together

scipy's PermutationMethod() is exhaustive -- and therefore deterministic -- only while 2**n <= its default n_resamples of 9999, i.e. n <= 13; above that it is an unseeded Monte-Carlo test whose p-value changes run to run (verified: two runs of this capture differed in the third decimal for n >= 14). That is why the selector caps the permutation branch at n = 13 and falls back to the normal approximation above it, and why the reimplementation must NOT extend exhaustive enumeration past the point where it is affordable and then silently sample instead.
